title: Judge Blocks Sony's Bid to Add 30,000 Songs to Udio AI Lawsuit
excerpt: A federal judge denied Sony Music's request to massively expand its copyright case against AI music generator Udio, keeping the suit limited to 333 works as the label stands alone among majors still litigating.
body:
• A federal judge denied Sony Music's request to add 30,442 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against AI music generator Udio, keeping the case limited to 333 works.
  • Sony is the last remaining major label plaintiff after Universal Music Group, Warner Music Group, Merlin, and Kobalt all reached licensing deals with Udio.
  • Sony used Audible Magic audio fingerprinting technology to identify what it called "hundreds of thousands" of copyrighted works in Udio's training data.
  • The case is heading toward summary judgment on the fair use question, with a ruling that could set legal precedent for the entire AI music industry.

Judge Blocks Sony's Bid to Expand Case

US District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein has denied Sony Music Entertainment's motion to add more than 30,000 copyrighted sound recordings to its copyright infringement lawsuit against AI music platform Udio, keeping the case at the 333 works from its original filing.

"Adding more than 30,000 works near the close of document discovery would require substantial additional production and review, generate further disputes, and materially alter the scope of the case before me," Hellerstein wrote in his ruling.

Sony filed the motion on May 22 in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, arguing it had identified the additional recordings after gaining access to Udio's training data during discovery. The label used audio recognition technology from Audible Magic to scan Udio's dataset, claiming to have found "hundreds of thousands" of copyrighted audio files used without permission.

"Plaintiffs have a sufficient basis to assert claims against Udio as to all the works they own or control that returned match results within Udio's training data."

— Sony Music, court filing

"US copyright law caps statutory damages at $150,000 per work for willful infringement, meaning the 30,442 works could have carried liability exceeding $4.5 billion."

Sony Stands Alone Among Major Labels

Sony Music, along with subsidiaries Arista Music and Arista Records, is now the sole remaining major-label plaintiff suing Udio. The lawsuit originated in June 2024, when the Recording Industry Association of America sued both Udio and rival Suno on behalf of all three major labels, accusing the platforms of "mass infringement."

Since then, the other majors have taken a different path. Universal Music Group settled with Udio in October 2025, reaching a licensing deal for a planned AI music service. Warner Music Group followed in November 2025 with its own licensing agreement. Independent licensing body Merlin struck a deal in January 2026, publisher Kobalt followed in April, and the National Music Publishers' Association announced what it called the "first-ever industry-wide licensing deal with a major AI music company" in June 2026.

Sony's decision to continue litigating places it at odds with the broader industry direction. Sony Music Group Chairman Rob Stringer has maintained that "direct licensing in advance of launching new products is the only appropriate way to build them," according to Music Business Worldwide.

Fair Use Battle Heads Toward Key Ruling

With its expansion blocked, Sony's case narrows but sharpens. At stake is the central legal question: whether training an AI model on copyrighted music constitutes fair use under US law.

Udio has argued that any copying of copyrightable expression in its training process is "quintessential fair use," describing its tool as a "back-end technological process, invisible to the public," that produces a non-infringing new product. The company admitted in its April answer that it "obtained audio data from YouTube for use as training data," while arguing that downloading publicly available videos is not unlawful.

Sony scored an early procedural win in April when Hellerstein declined to dismiss its claim that Udio circumvented YouTube's technological protections against stream-ripping — a Digital Millennium Copyright Act allegation that adds another dimension to the case.

Had the judge approved the expansion, Udio's potential damages exposure would have ballooned. US copyright law caps statutory damages at $150,000 per work for willful infringement, meaning the 30,442 works could have carried liability exceeding $4.5 billion. With the case limited to 333 works, maximum statutory exposure sits around $50 million.

Broader Implications for Music and AI

The case carries significance beyond the immediate parties. A parallel lawsuit against Suno — pursued jointly by Sony and Universal in Massachusetts — involves 61,026 recordings, with document production closing on August 25. Both cases are expected to produce summary judgment motions on the fair use question that could shape the legal framework for AI music generation globally.

For Indian music rights holders, including major players like T-Series and Saregama with vast catalogs of copyrighted content, the outcome could establish precedents affecting how AI companies worldwide use copyrighted recordings. India's music industry, which generated $360 million in recorded music revenue in 2024 according to IFPI, faces similar questions about AI training on copyrighted works as generative music tools expand into regional markets.

Meanwhile, Udio is reportedly preparing to relaunch its platform later this year as a walled-garden service with authorized content. Whether Sony ultimately settles or pushes for a court ruling may depend on how the fair use arguments develop as both sides prepare for summary judgment — a decision that the entire music industry is watching closely.
nri_angle: Indian music rights holders including T-Series and Saregama face similar questions about AI training on copyrighted works; the case could set global precedents for how AI companies use copyrighted recordings from regional markets.
